blocks.text: Apple does not read your description when ranking search. It indexes exactly three fields: title (30 chars), subtitle (30) and the hidden keyword field (100). Each word is indexed once, whichever field it sits in. Title words weigh most, subtitle medium, keyword field least.
What Apple adds up to decide who ranks first

items: Text relevance: every word of the query must exist across your three fields. If one is missing, you do not exist for that phrase.
Conversion: how many people who see your card actually install. Icon, first two screenshots and subtitle decide it.
Ratings and rating velocity: an app with 100 new ratings a month overtakes one with 5,000 old ones. That is why the Overview draws your ratings velocity.
Downloads from that phrase: the more people install after typing “habit tracker”, the higher you rank for it. This is where Search Ads come in.

blocks.text: The two-word phrase “habit reminder” ranks if you have “habit” in the title and “reminder” in the keyword field. You never need to repeat the whole phrase. That is why the Audit checks coverage word by word.
Apple ignores “app”, “free”, category names and plurals when you already have the singular. Every such character is wasted.

title: How to read the numbers on this page

items.label: Position
items.text: Your app’s place in the results for that phrase in that country. “—” means below 200. Almost nobody sees below 10; below 30 you practically do not exist.

items.label: Traffic (0–100)
items.text: How much the phrase is searched. Derived from Apple autocomplete (a phrase Apple suggests while typing is a phrase people type), result count and length. 80+ is a head term, below 30 is long tail.

items.label: Difficulty (0–100)
items.text: How strong the top 10 apps are, measured by rating counts. 90 means the top 10 is held by apps with 100,000+ ratings. Below 40 is ground you can take in weeks.

items.label: Opportunity
items.text: Traffic minus difficulty. Green (+20 and up) are the keywords to focus on. Red is held by giants and you do not enter without budget.

items.label: Visibility
items.text: Sum of traffic × position over all tracked keywords. One number that says whether ASO is moving. Watch the trend, not the daily value.

blocks.text: No ASO tool has Apple’s real traffic numbers, because Apple does not publish them. Applyra, AppTweak and we all estimate. The relation between keywords is right; the absolute value is a guide.
Your best keywords today: traffic 40–80, difficulty under 55, position under 100 or “—” but covered in your fields. Those are the ones where a title tweak and 50 new ratings make the difference.

items.title: Monday · Overview (5 min)
items.text: Read Insights and Biggest movers. A drop of 10+ places on a keyword with traffic 60+ is the only thing that needs a same-day reaction.

items.title: Wednesday · Discovery (10 min)
items.text: One seed, one brainstorm or one competitor mining run. Track only keywords with opportunity +15 and relevance 50%+.

items.title: Friday · Competitors (3 min)
items.text: Listing changes. If a competitor changed its subtitle, watch which keywords it jumps on next week and learn.

items.title: Monthly · Audit + AI (15 min)
items.text: Refresh the keyword field, generate an AI proposal, compare with the live listing. Change the listing at most every 4–6 weeks so you can measure the effect.

blocks.text: Do not change title and subtitle more than once a month. Apple needs 7–14 days to reindex and you need two more weeks to see movement. Change constantly and you never know what worked.

title: Strategy: long tail before the head

blocks.text: For “habit tracker” (traffic 84, difficulty 90) you sit at position 98. Habitica up there has 161,000 ratings. That keyword is not won with copy, it is won over years. So the strategy has three layers.

items.title: Layer 1 · The niche nobody defends
items.text: ADHD, sleep routine, fasting routine, UTI habit. Difficulty 20–45. You can reach top 5 in weeks because you are the only habit tracker with medical protocols. These words go in the title or subtitle.

items.title: Layer 2 · Feature phrases
items.text: apple watch habit, habit widget, siri habit log, habit reminder alarm. Medium difficulty, people typing them know what they want and convert easily. They go in the keyword field.

items.title: Layer 3 · Category head
items.text: habit tracker, daily habits, routine. You are present through title words and you will grow there only once layers 1 and 2 bring ratings and installs. Do not pay ads for them until you are organically under 30.

blocks.text: One good niche word in the title beats three generic ones. “Habitly: Habit & ADHD” makes you the only result for a query everyone on Ozempic types.

items: Seed: type one word and Apple autocomplete expands in depth. The best seed is a problem, not a product: “ozempic”, “sleep”, “fasting”, “headache” instead of “habit app”.
From competitors: we take the words competitors put in titles and subtitles and check which phrases Apple actually suggests. If three competitors have “reminder”, that is the word the market uses.
AI brainstorm: the model proposes 30 phrases from the user’s angle (situations, diagnoses, devices), then Apple data decides which are worth it. Great for languages you do not speak.

blocks.text: Every candidate gets relevance: the share of top-10 apps from Health & Fitness, Medical, Lifestyle or Food & Drink. “habit eject” scores 0% because those are speaker cleaners. Never track off-niche words no matter the traffic.
Track a keyword only when it has opportunity +15 and relevance 50%+. Tracking costs time (4 seconds per keyword per country per day) and above 60 keywords per country the overview gets noisy.

Every day we snapshot each competitor’s title, subtitle, version and description. When something changes, the Overview shows it. A competitor with 100,000 ratings does not change its subtitle without a reason: it tested and found a better word, or it is chasing a new niche.

items: The keywords table shows competitor positions next to yours. A keyword where every competitor is top 10 and you are not is one the market considers basic. You must cover it.
A keyword where no competitor is in the top 10 (e.g. “sleep routine”) is empty ground. Those are won first.
Add small competitors with 500–5,000 ratings too. They show what is realistic for you in 6 months; giants show what is realistic in 3 years.

head: Field
Limit
Weight
Rule
rows: Brand + 1–2 most important words. No punctuation eating characters.
Words NOT in the title. A readable sentence, users see it.
Commas without spaces. No plurals, no title/subtitle words, no “app” or “free”, no competitor brands.

blocks.text: Apple never publishes the keyword field, so paste it from App Store Connect (App Information → Keywords) into the Audit. Without it the audit sees 60 of 160 characters.
The trick most people skip: extra localizations

The US storefront also indexes Spanish (Mexico), Arabic, Russian and Chinese. If you add a Spanish (Mexico) localization in App Store Connect with DIFFERENT keywords in English (no translation needed), you get another 160 indexed characters for the same country. The UK also indexes Australian English. The AI proposal gives you secondary localizations for exactly this.
A word is indexed once. “Tracker” in both title and subtitle is 7 wasted characters. The Audit calls these duplicates.

title: AI proposal: use it without copying blindly

blocks.text: The model receives your listing, every position and score, the audit and your competitors. It returns title, subtitle and keyword field within Apple limits, with a rationale for each decision. It is good at combinatorics (which word where so everything is covered); you are better at what is true for your app.

items.title: 1. Read the rationales, not just the proposal
items.text: If it drops “tracker” from the subtitle because of a duplicate, that is right. If it proposes a word for a feature you do not have, strike it.

items.title: 2. Compare with coverage in the Audit
items.text: The proposal should reduce the number of uncovered tracked phrases. If it does not, tell it in the notes which keywords are your priority.

items.title: 3. Apply one change a month
items.text: Keyword field first (lowest risk, users never see it). If visibility rises within 2 weeks, subtitle next month. Title last.

blocks.text: The note to the model changes everything. “Focus on ADHD, do not mention fasting, keep the brand first” yields a better proposal than any button.

title: Apple Search Ads: pay only for the right words

blocks.text: Search Ads are the ads at the top of App Store search. You pay per tap (CPT), not per install. Average CPT in Health & Fitness is $1–2.5 and an install costs $2–5. Without a plan, the budget goes to “habit tracker” where you pay $3 a tap against Habitica and gain nothing lasting.
Exact or Broad?

Exact means you pay for that exact query and its close variants (plurals, typos). Broad means Apple expands to related queries and synonyms, cheaper per tap, but you also pay for things you did not ask for. Rule: everything proven or close to the top (Defend, Accelerate, Niche) goes Exact into one campaign. Everything you are testing goes Broad into a separate Discovery campaign with a low bid, together with Search Match. Add every Exact keyword to Discovery as a Negative Exact, otherwise Broad steals your proven queries and pollutes your data. When Broad or Search Match finds a query that converts, move it to the first campaign as Exact. The Search Ads tab already does this in the CSV.
How the Search Ads tab groups keywords

head: Group
When
Why pay
Bid
rows: So a competitor cannot buy your keyword and brand. Cheap, because you are relevant.
Paid installs from that phrase lift the organic position. Most of the budget goes here.
Nobody bids, a tap costs $0.5, the user knows what they want.
Small daily cap to see TTR and conversion before investing.
You pay the most expensive taps against 100k-rating apps with no lasting effect.

items.title: Week 1
items.text: Launch Accelerate and Niche, exact match, daily cap $5–10. Add all off-niche words as negatives in the Search Match campaign.

items.title: Week 2
items.text: Watch TTR (tap-through rate) and CR (conversion rate). TTR under 5% means your card does not attract for that word: change screenshots, not the bid. CR under 30% means the word is not your audience: pause it.

items.title: Weeks 3–4
items.text: Keywords with CPA (cost per install) under $3 get a higher bid. Above $6 get paused. Compare organic positions with the Overview: if a paid keyword jumped 10+ places organically, it is a keyword that pays off.

blocks.text: The CSV from the Search Ads tab imports directly into Apple Search Ads (Campaigns → Import). Negative keywords are already in it.
Never pay for a word you do not have in any of the three fields. Apple assigns a lower relevance score and charges more per tap.

title: Conversion and ratings: half the rank

blocks.text: Search position is half the battle. The other half is how many people who see you install, and how many leave a rating afterwards. Apple measures both per keyword.

items: Icon and the first two screenshots show in search results without opening the page. The first screenshot must say what the app does in one second, with 3–5 words of text.
Ratings: ask at a moment of success (goal met, 7-day streak), not on launch. Apple allows 3 prompts a year per user through SKStoreReviewController.
Product Page Optimization in App Store Connect: A/B test icon and screenshots with real traffic. Change one thing per test, run 2 weeks.
In-App Events show in search as separate cards. A “ADHD routine week” event is free visibility for the niche.

blocks.text: The Overview draws new ratings per day. Aim for a steady trend, not a spike. One new rating a day in month one, 3–5 by year end, changes the difficulty you can attack.
